title: Definition
body_md:
A {\bf soft inductive system} $(E,j)$ of normed spaces over a directed set $(N,\le)$ is a net of normed spaces $\{E_n\}_{n\in N}$ together with linear contractions $j_{nm}:E_m\to E_n$ defined if $n>m$, which are asymptotically transitive:
    \begin{equation}
        \IfNoValueTF{_}{\mathop{\textup{lim}}}{{_}\!-\!\mathop{\textup{lim}}}{n\gg m} \norm{(j_{nl}-j_{nm}j_{ml})a_l} = 0, \qquad l\in N,\ a_l\in E_l,
    \end{equation}
    where we use the notation $\IfNoValueTF{_}{\mathop{\textup{lim}}}{{_}\!-\!\mathop{\textup{lim}}}{n\gg m}$ as a shorthand for $\IfNoValueTF{_}{\mathop{\textup{lim}}}{{_}\!-\!\mathop{\textup{lim}}}m \varlimsup_n$.
    If each $E_n$ is a Banach space, we call $(E,j)$ a soft inductive system of Banach spaces. 
    A {\bf soft inductive sequence} of normed (Banach) spaces is a soft inductive system $(E,j)$ with index set $N=\mathbb N$ (with the usual order).

label: rem:summable to coherent
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:summable to coherent}
   In \cite[Remark 2.1.4]{blackadar1997generalized} soft inductive systems are alluded to under the name of asymptotically coherent systems. 
   When the index is countable, it is sometimes useful to consider a stronger notion: 
    A soft inductive system $(E,j)$ which is indexed over $\mathbb{N}$ is \emph{summably soft} if  there exists some decreasing sequence $(\varepsilon_n)_n\in \ell^1(\mathbb{N})_+^1$ such that 
    \begin{align*}
        \|j_{nk}-j_{nm}\circ j_{mk}\|<\varepsilon_m,\ \forall\ n>m>k\geq 0.
    \end{align*}

    

Now, suppose $(E,j)$ is a summably soft inductive system of vector spaces. We define a strict system $(E,{\ensuremath{\tilde\jmath}})$ from $(E,j)$ as follows: for all $n>m\geq 0$ set
\begin{align*}
    {\ensuremath{\tilde\jmath}}_{nm}&\coloneqq j_{n,n-1}\circ\hdots\circ j_{m+1,m},\\
    {\ensuremath{\tilde\jmath}}_{mn}&\coloneqq 0,\ \text{ and}\\
    {\ensuremath{\tilde\jmath}}_{nn}&\coloneqq \mathrm{id}_{E_n}.
\end{align*}
It follows from summability that for any $\varepsilon>0$ there exists an $M>0$ such that for all $n>m>M$, 
$$\|{\ensuremath{\tilde\jmath}}_{nm}-j_{nm}\|<\varepsilon.$$
In particular, $\|{\ensuremath{\tilde\jmath}}_{\infty n}-j_{\oon}\|<\varepsilon$ for each $n>M$.  
Then 
\[\overline{\bigcup {\ensuremath{\tilde\jmath}}_{\infty n}(E_n)}=\overline{\bigcup j_{\oon}(E_n)}\subset {\mathbf Q}(E_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}}),\]
and we denote both with $E'_\infty$.  

If $(E,j)$ is a summably soft system of finite-dimensional Banach spaces with countable index, we can use a compactness argument to pass to an asymptotically soft subsystem whose limit is isometrically isomorphic to $E'_\infty$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:subsystem limit}.

body_md:
\label{prop:upropunital}
    Every unital completely positive map $\varphi:\mathcal T_1\to\mathcal T_2$ that vanishes on ${\mathcal J}$, ${\mathcal J}\subset\ker(\varphi)$, factors through the quotient.
    That is, the map $\hat\varphi:\mathcal T_1/{\mathcal J}\to\mathcal T_2$ with $\hat\varphi(x+{\mathcal J}) = \varphi(x)$ is well-defined, unital and completely positive.
    
    Let $\mathcal R$ be an operator system and $\psi:\mathcal T_1\to\mathcal R$ a unital completely positive map.
    If it holds that for every unital completely positive map $\varphi:\mathcal T_1\to\mathcal T_2$ with ${\mathcal J}\subset \ker(\varphi)$ there exists a unique unital completely positive map $\hat\varphi:\mathcal R\to\mathcal T_2$ such that $\varphi = \hat\varphi\circ\psi$ then there exists a unique complete order isomorphism $\gamma:\mathcal R\to\mathcal T_1/{\mathcal J}$ such that $\gamma\circ\psi$ is the canonical quotient map.

Let $\varphi:\mathcal T_1\to\mathcal T_2$ be a contractive completely positive map. Then we can view $\varphi$ as a unital completely positive map $\mathcal T_1\to\varphi(\mathcal T_1) =: \mathcal T$ where we choose $\varphi(1_{\mathcal T_1}) =: 1_{\mathcal T}$ as the order unit of $\mathcal T$.
        The universal property Proposition~\ref{prop:upropunital} then gives existence of a unique unital completely positive map $\hat\varphi:\mathcal T_1/{\mathcal J}\to\mathcal T$ necessarily given by $\hat\varphi(x+{\mathcal J}) = \varphi(x)$.
        Note that, since $\varphi$ is contractive, it holds that $\norm{1_{\mathcal T}}_{\mathcal T_2} \le \norm{1_{\mathcal T_1}}_{\mathcal T_1} = 1 = \norm{1_{\mathcal T}}_\mathcal T$, so the embedding $\mathcal T\hookrightarrow\mathcal T_2$ is contractive.
        Thus, viewing $\hat\varphi$ as a map $\mathcal T_1/{\mathcal J}\to\mathcal T_2$ gives a completely positive contraction.

By \cite[Prop. 3.1]{kavruk2013quotients} it suffices to find a family of states $\Omega$ on $\mathbf{C}(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}},j)$ such that $\mathbf{C}_0(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}})=\bigcap_{\psi\in\Omega}\ker\psi$.
    Let $\omega$ be an ultrafilter on $N$ that is compatible with the order structure in the sense that it contains all cofinite sets in $N$. 
    \footnote{A subset $M$ of a directed set $(N,\le)$ is cofinal if every element of $N$ is dominated by some element of $M$. To see that such a filter exists, consider the filter of all cofinite sets and pick any ultrafilter $\omega$ containing it. These filters are free (or non-principal) if and only if $N$ does not contain a maximal element.}
    Let $\psi_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}}$ be \emph{any} net of states (i.e., $\psi_n$ is a state on $\mathcal S_n$ for all $n$). 
    Then one obtains a state $\psi_{\omega}$ on $\mathbf{C}(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}},j)$ which maps a \ensuremath{j_{}}-convergent net $a_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}}$ to $\IfNoValueTF{_}{\mathop{\textup{lim}}}{{_}\!-\!\mathop{\textup{lim}}}{n\to\omega} \psi_n(a_n)$. 
    We set $\Omega = \{\psi_\omega : \psi_n\in S_n,\ n\in N, \ \omega\}$, where "$\omega$" ranges over all order-compatible ultrafilters on $N$.
    It is clear that any null net $a_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}}$ is in the kernel of any such state, i.e., $\mathbf{C}_0(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}})\subset \bigcap_{\psi\in\Omega}\ker \psi$. 
    Conversely, assume that a, without loss of generality, self-adjoint net $a_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}}=a_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}}^*$ is in the kernel of all $\psi\in\Omega$.
    Pick a net of states $\psi_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}}$ such that $\norm{a_n}=\abs{\psi_n(a_n)}$.

body_md:
{\cite[Proposition 5.12]{kavruk2013quotients}}\label{prop:Kav+5.12}
    Let $\mathcal{I}$ be an ideal of a $\mathrm{C}^*$-algebra $\mathcal A$, $\{e_\alpha\}_\alpha$ be a quasi-central approximate unit for $\mathcal{I}$ and $\mathcal S\subset \mathcal A$ be an operator system. If $e_\alpha s\in {\mathcal J}=\mathcal S\cap \mathcal{I}$ for every $s\in \mathcal S$ and for every $\alpha$, then the induced map $\mathcal S/{\mathcal J}\to \mathcal A/\mathcal{I}$ is a (unital) complete order isomorphism. The operator space and operator system quotients $\mathcal S/{\mathcal J}$ are completely isometric and ${\mathcal J}$ is a completely biproximinal kernel in $\mathcal S$.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:nuclearity_iff}
    Let $\mathcal S$ be a nuclear operator system, then $\mathcal S$ is a soft inductive limit of matrix algebras, i.e., there is a soft inductive system $(\mathcal S,j)$ with each $\mathcal S_n$ being a matrix algebra so that $\mathcal S$ is its limit space.

    If $\mathcal S$ is separable, then the directed system can be chosen to be $N=\mathbb N$, and the soft inductive system can be arranged to be strict.

title: Proof
body_md:
Given a net of completely positive contractions $\varphi_n:\mathcal S\to M_{\nu_n}$ and $\psi_n:M_{\nu_n}\to\mathcal S$ such that $\varphi_n\circ\psi_n$ converges point norm to $\operatorname{id}_\mathcal S$, we form the induced soft inductive system 
   $(\mathcal S,j)$ as above. The limit space $\mathcal S_\infty$ is  completely order isomorphic  with $\mathcal S$ via $a \mapsto \ensuremath{j_{}}\mkern-1mu\hbox{-}\mkern-3mu\IfNoValueTF{_}{\mathop{\textup{lim}}}{{_}\!-\!\mathop{\textup{lim}}}n \psi_n(a)$ (the inverse is $\ensuremath{j_{}}\mkern-1mu\hbox{-}\mkern-3mu\IfNoValueTF{_}{\mathop{\textup{lim}}}{{_}\!-\!\mathop{\textup{lim}}}n a_n \mapsto \IfNoValueTF{_}{\mathop{\textup{lim}}}{{_}\!-\!\mathop{\textup{lim}}}n \varphi_n(a_n)$).
    With this identification of $\mathcal S$ and $\mathcal S_\infty$ we get $j_{\oon}=\varphi_n$. 
                                                 

  When $\mathcal S$ is separable, 
                                                                                                                                                 
   the index set can be chosen to be $\mathbb{N}$ by sequentially choosing better and better cpc approximations for a nested sequence of finite subsets of $\mathcal S$ whose union is dense in $\mathcal S$. One can then use a compactness argument (such as in \cite[Remark 3.2(ii)]{CW1}), to further refine this resulting sequence $\mathcal S\xrightarrow{\psi_n}M_{\nu_n}\xrightarrow{\varphi_n}\mathcal S$ of cpc approximations to one satisfying 
   \[\|\varphi_m-\varphi_n\circ \psi_n\circ\varphi_m\|<\frac{1}{2^n}, \text{ for all } n>m\geq 0.\]   (This is called a \emph{summable} system of cpc approximations in \cite{CW1}.) 
   Summability of the cpc approximations 
   implies summability of the induced soft inductive system $j_{nm}=\psi_n\circ\varphi_m:M_{\nu_m}\to M_{\nu_n}$. And so, as in Remark~\ref{rem:summable to coherent}, we can form a strict system ${\ensuremath{\tilde\jmath}}_{nm:}=\psi_n\circ\varphi_{n-1}\circ\hdots \circ \psi_{m+1}\circ\varphi_m:M_{\nu_m}\to M_{\nu_n}$ with the same limit.

title: Lemma
body_md: Let $\mathcal A$ be a $C^*$-algebra with two-sided closed ideal ${\mathcal J}$, and let $\mathcal S\subset \mathcal A$ be an operator system which contains ${\mathcal J}$. Then $(\mathcal S/{\mathcal J})^{**}$ is completely order isomorphic to $p^\perp \mathcal S^{**}$ where $p$ is the central support projection of ${\mathcal J}$. (In fact, we have $\mathcal S^{**}\cong {\mathcal J}^{**}\oplus (\mathcal S/{\mathcal J})^{**}$.)
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For each $\varphi\in S(\mathcal A)$, write $(\sigma_\varphi, H_\varphi, \xi_\varphi)$ for the associated cyclic GNS representation. Write $H_\mathcal A:=\bigoplus_{\varphi\in S(\mathcal A)} H_\varphi$ and let 
$\sigma_u:\mathcal A\to B(H_\mathcal A)$ be the universal representation for $\mathcal A$. Since ${\mathcal J}$ is an ideal in $\mathcal A$, its essential support $\overline{\sigma_u({\mathcal J})H_\mathcal A}$  is invariant under $\sigma_u(\mathcal A)$, and so its orthogonal projection $p$ (which is the SOT limit of an increasing approximate identity in ${\mathcal J}$) lies in $\sigma_u(\mathcal A)'\cap \sigma_u(\mathcal A)''$. Hence we have 
\[\sigma_u(\mathcal A)''=p\sigma_u(\mathcal A)''\oplus p^\perp \sigma_u(\mathcal A)''.\]
Note that the orthogonal complement of $\overline{\sigma_u({\mathcal J})H_\mathcal A}$ is $\bigoplus_{{\mathcal J}\subset \text{ker}(\sigma_\varphi), \varphi\in S(\mathcal A)} H_\varphi$ (i.e., the largest subspace on which $\sigma_u(x)=0$ for all $x\in {\mathcal J}$).

We can identify $\mathcal A/{\mathcal J}$ with $p^\perp \sigma_u(\mathcal A)$ via the map $\pi:\mathcal A/{\mathcal J}\to B(p^\perp H_\mathcal A)$ given by $\pi(a+{\mathcal J})=\oplus_{{\mathcal J}\subset \text{ker}(\sigma_\varphi), \varphi\in S(\mathcal A)}$. Since every (GNS) representation of $\mathcal A/{\mathcal J}$ extends to a (GNS) representation of $\mathcal A$ which vanishes on ${\mathcal J}$ (by composing with the quotient map), we can identify $\pi(\mathcal A/{\mathcal J})$ with the image of $\mathcal A/{\mathcal J}$ under its universal representaion. In particular, that means we can identify $(\mathcal A/{\mathcal J})^{**}\cong \pi(\mathcal A/{\mathcal J})''=p^\perp \sigma_u(\mathcal A)''$. We can also write $p\sigma_u(\mathcal A)''\cong {\mathcal J}^{**}$ (though that is not important here), and, by identifying $\sigma_u(\mathcal A)''\cong \mathcal A^{**}$, we have 
\[\mathcal A^{**}\cong p\mathcal A^{**}\oplus p^\perp \mathcal A^{**}\cong {\mathcal J}^{**}\oplus (\mathcal A/{\mathcal J})^{**}.\]

Since $\mathcal S\subset \mathcal A$, we have $p^\perp \mathcal S^{**}\subset p^\perp \mathcal A^{**}$. We just need to argue that $p^\perp \mathcal S^{**}$ is mapped to $(\mathcal S/{\mathcal J})^{**}$ under the identification $p^\perp \mathcal A^{**}\cong (\mathcal A/{\mathcal J})^{**}$. Since $p^\perp \mathcal S=\pi(\mathcal S/{\mathcal J})$, we know that $p^\perp \mathcal S$ gets sent to $\mathcal S/{\mathcal J}$ in this identification. Since $\mathcal S$ and $\mathcal S/{\mathcal J}$ are ultraweakly (wk$^*$) dense in $\mathcal S^{**}$ and $(\mathcal S/{\mathcal J})^{**}$, respectively,                                     
and since multiplication by a central projection and the above identification $p^\perp \mathcal A^{**}\cong (\mathcal A/{\mathcal J})^{**}$ are ultraweakly (wk$^*$) continuous, it follows that 
$p^\perp \mathcal S^{**}$ gets sent to $(\mathcal S/{\mathcal J})^{**}$ under the identification $p^\perp \mathcal A^{**}\cong (\mathcal A/{\mathcal J})^{**}$. Since this identification is a $^*$-isomorphism, its restriction and co-restriction gives a complete order isomorphism between $(\mathcal S/{\mathcal J})^{**}$ and  $p^\perp \mathcal S^{**}$.

label: lem: nuc quotient
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem: nuc quotient}
    Let $\mathcal A$ be a $C^*$-algebra with two-sided closed ideal ${\mathcal J}$, and let $\mathcal S\subset \mathcal A$ be a separable nuclear operator system which contains ${\mathcal J}$. Then $\mathcal S/{\mathcal J}$ is nuclear.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It follows from \cite{CE77,EOR01,Kir95} that an operator system is nuclear if and only if its double dual is completely order isomorphic to an injective von Neumann algebra. (See \cite[Theorem 3.5]{han2011approximation} for a proof.) Then $\mathcal S^{**}$ is injective. Letting $p$ denote the central support projection of ${\mathcal J}$, we have $\mathcal S^{**}\cong p\mathcal S^{**}\oplus p^\perp \mathcal S^{**}$, and so compression by $p^\perp$ is a conditional expectation onto $p^\perp \mathcal S^{**}$. Then $p^\perp \mathcal S^{**}$ is also injective, and hence so is $(\mathcal S/{\mathcal J})^{**}$. Since it is injective, we know from \cite{CE77} that it is completely order isomorphic to a $C^*$-algebra, which is moreover a double dual and thus a von Neumann algebra by Sakai's theorem \cite[Thm.~1.16.7]{sakai_c-algebras_1998}. 
    Hence $(\mathcal S/{\mathcal J})^{**}$ is completely order isomorphic to a von Neumann algebra, which (by \cite[Lemma 2.8 (ii)]{Kir95}) implies that $\mathcal S/{\mathcal J}$ is a nuclear operator system.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
This is not true for general quotients of operator systems. In \cite[Section 2]{FP12}, Farenick and Paulsen consider the operator system $M_n/{\mathcal J}_n$ for $n>2$ where \[{\mathcal J}_n=\{d\in M_n\mid d\text{ diagonal and } \text{tr}_n(D)=0\}.\] They show (\cite[Theorem 2.6]{FP12}) this is completely order isomorphic to the operator system 
    \[W_n=\text{span}\{w_iw_j^*\mid 1\leq i,j\leq n\}\subset C^*(\mathbb{F}_{n-1})\] where $w_2,...,w_n$ are the unitaries in $C^*(\mathbb{F}_{n-1})$ corresponding to the generators of $\mathbb{F}_{n-1}$ and $w_1=1$. Moreover, in the same theorem, they show that the enveloping $C^*$-algebra $C^*_e(W_n)$ is $C^*(\mathbb{F}_{n-1})$. Since $W_n\subset C^*(\mathbb{F}_{n-1})$ has enough unitaries (meaning $\mathcal{U}(C^*(\mathbb{F}_{n-1}))\cap W_n$ generates $C^*(\mathbb{F}_{n-1})$ as a $C^*$-algebra) and since $C^*(\mathbb{F}_{n-1})$ is non-exact, it follows from \cite[Corollary 9.6]{kavruk2013quotients}, that $W_n$ is not (min,el)-nuclear. By the hierarchy of operator system tensor products, this implies that $W_n$ is also not (max,min)-nuclear, which we here call nuclear.

\label{lem: preimage is nuc}
Let $(\mathcal S,j)$ be a strict inductive sequence such that $\mathcal S_n=M_{k_n}$ for each $n\in \mathbb{N}$. title: Proof
body_md:
To show $\mathbf{C}(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}},j)\subset {\mathbf{N}}(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}})=\prod_n M_{k_n}$ is nuclear, we present a sequence of completely positive approximations through matrix algebras. For each $m\in \mathbb{N}$, let $\psi_m:\mathbf{C}(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}},j)\to \bigoplus_{j=1}^m M_{k_j}$ be the restriction of the canonical compression $\prod_n M_{k_n}\to \bigoplus_{j=1}^m M_{k_j}$ to $\mathbf{C}(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}},j)$, and let $\varphi_m:\bigoplus_{j=1}^m M_{k_j}\to \prod_n M_{k_n}$ be defined for $(x_1,...,x_m)\in \bigoplus_{j=1}^m M_{k_j}$ as 
    \[(x_1,...,x_m)\mapsto (x_1,...,x_m,j_{_m+1,m}(x_m),j_{_m+2,m}(x_m),...).\]
   Note that we can identify $\mathbf{C}(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}},j)$ with the closure of the set 
\[X_0:=\{(x_n)_n\in \prod_n M_{k_n} : \exists\ m\geq 1, x_{n+1}=j_{_n+1,n}(x_n), \forall\ n\geq m\}.\]
Hence the image of $\varphi_m$ clearly lies in $\mathbf{C}(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}},j)$, and to check nuclearity, we only need to check it for $(x_n)_n\in X_0$. For such a sequence, we choose $m>0$ such that for all $n\geq m$, $j_{_n+1,n}(x_n)=x_{n+1}$. Then for all $n\geq m$, we have $\varphi_n(\psi_n(x))=x$. It follows that $\mathbf{C}(\mathcal S_{{\hspace{0.0pt}{\mathbin{{\hbox{\scalebox{0.7}{$\,\begin{picture}(-1,1)(-1,-2.5)\circle*{3}\end{picture}\,\,\, $}}}}}\hspace{+0pt}}{\hspace{-1pt}}},j)$ is nuclear.
